reasoning_traces.think:
The additive feedback model posits that goal-scoring probability evolves according to p(n) = p(n−1) + κ, implying a drift toward higher goal counts over time. In the continuum limit, this leads to a negative binomial distribution with parameters r = p0/κ and p = 1 − e^{−κt}. This derivation shows how discrete-time feedback mechanisms can generate heavy-tailed distributions typical of real-world sports scoring. The key insight is that while the model assumes stationarity and ignores team-specific heterogeneity, it still captures overdispersion through its dependence on κ. The empirical validation reveals weak negative correlations between home and away goals, suggesting that any perceived momentum is likely due to unmodeled variance in team strength rather than true in-match contagion. Thus, the model serves as a foundational benchmark for score modeling but must be extended with hierarchical structures to account for real-world complexity.
